variant_decisions.evidence: ASV opens the verse 'If any man thinketh' with no connective. A postpositive de is routinely left untranslated in the ASV, so its absence in English neither attests nor excludes it; nothing else in the verse distinguishes ei from ei de.
ASV renders 'thinketh that he knoweth anything'. Both egnokenai and eidenai are rendered 'know' in the ASV, and no note is mapped here, so the English does not distinguish the two infinitives.

ASV has 'he knoweth not yet as he ought to know', a bare negated verb with no object. The RP reading oudepo ouden supplies an accusative 'nothing/anything' that the ASV does not render; the only 'anything' in the verse belongs to the preceding infinitive clause (ti egnokenai). The absence of a second object distinguishes oupo.

ASV 'he knoweth not yet' gives no tense signal that separates the aorist egno from the perfect egnoken; the ASV renders both aorist and perfect of ginosko with an English present here, and no note is mapped to this unit.

The clause is verbless with a noun subject and a negative predicate, so the supplied copula goes to the predicate (rules 53, 63). The ASV recasts the predicate οὐδέν as the discontinuous negation no … anything, both words realizing this one token under rule 15; marking the italicized anything added under rule 103 remains defensible, but nothing else licenses it and οὐδέν's own English is what it completes. This is why this clause is not analysed like the verse's second one: here the negative is the predicate, whereas οὐδείς below is attributive to its noun.

ἐν → in; the prepositional phrase is an adjunct here rather than the predicate, the ASV's own complement of the copula being anything, so rule 53's preposition carrier does not apply and the copula stays with οὐδέν.
Anarthrous κόσμῳ with a supplied determiner: no article competes, so the is an ordinary helper on the noun (rule 51).

Verbless existential clause expressing no subject of its own: the supplied subject there and the copula is ride with the predicate noun (rule 68), discontinuously across the attributive quantifier under rule 15. This is the same analysis this chapter gives εἷς θεός → there is one God at 1CO.8.6, and the same the corpus gives the identical frame at 1TI.2.5 (θεός → there is god, headed on the noun). Placing there is on οὐδείς remains defensible, but a quantifier standing inside the predicate phrase is a modifier and not the carrier, as rule 96 already holds for an article.

οὐδείς is attributive to θεός and keeps only its own English word no, exactly as εἷς keeps a bare one at 1CO.8.6. Rules 41, 59 and 87 decide where the English negation goes and say nothing about a supplied verb, so carrying the clause's negation does not make this token the carrier of the existential.
εἰ μή rendered by the single but: the conjunction answers to neither particle separately (rule 39), headed on the first particle and on the English word.

review_notes: The verse's two verbless clauses are analysed apart because the Greek differs, not because of the English. In οὐδὲν εἴδωλον ἐν κόσμῳ the negative is the clause's own predicate and rule 63 gives it the copula; in οὐδεὶς θεός the negative is attributive and θεός is the only nominal left, so the supplied existential rides with the noun under rule 68. The earlier reading, which placed there is on οὐδείς for parallelism with the first clause, split this chapter against 1CO.8.6's εἷς θεός → there is one God and against 1TI.2.5.

The italicized anything is folded onto οὐδέν rather than marked added: rule 103's test is licensing, and οὐδέν's own English is what the word completes. Marking it added remains defensible and is named here so a later reader can act on it.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV reads 'some, being used until now to the idol', which renders synetheiai (custom, habitual use). The RP syneidesei would give 'with conscience of the idol'; the ASV keeps 'conscience' for the separate syneidesis later in the verse ('their conscience being weak is defiled') and does not use it here.

The two readings differ only in the order of heos arti and tou eidolou; both say the same thing. English word order in 'being used until now to the idol' follows ASV clause construction, not the sequence of the Greek words, so it cannot attest either arrangement, and no note is mapped here.

review_notes: v009 is marked FALLBACK EXCLUDED BY EVIDENCE: the projection carries r00-base over s009–s017 while the evidence leaves r02 and r03, and the ASV plainly follows a reading in which the two conditional clauses stand in the reverse order (eat not / worse, then eat / better). Every token of the projection still has an English counterpart, so nothing here is added or unrepresented on that account and the difference is handled as reordering under rule 15; γάρ is unrepresented because the ASV writes no word for it, not on textual grounds. Rule 12 is untouched — no new textual decision is taken.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV reads 'food will not commend us to God' — a future. That renders the future parastesei, not the present paristesin. The mapped note 'Greek present.' glosses the sense of paristemi (to present) rather than a tense, so it does not tell against the future form.

ASV puts the abstaining clause first: 'neither, if we eat not, are we the worse; nor, if we eat, are we the better', and the mapped notes confirm the pairing ('Greek do we lack' on 'the worse' = hysteroumetha, 'Greek do we abound' on 'the better' = perisseuomen). That excludes r00-base and r01, which begin with eating and abounding, and the ASV also renders no 'for' (gar). Between r02 and r03 the English cannot distinguish the active perisseuomen from the middle perisseuometha, both rendered 'are we the better'.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV reads 'For ... he that is weak perisheth': a causal 'For' rendering gar and a present 'perisheth' rendering apollytai. The RP Kai apoleitai would give 'And ... shall perish', which matches neither the connective nor the tense the ASV prints.

The mapped note 'Greek in.' stands on 'through thy knowledge' and states the underlying preposition is en, which is the base reading; the RP alternative reads epi. The note also excludes the RP placement of adelphos before the prepositional phrase, since the ASV's 'the brother' follows 'through thy knowledge'.

ASV reads 'perisheth, the brother for whose sake Christ died' — an appositional 'the brother' after the knowledge phrase, which renders ho adelphos in the base position. RP omits the word here (having it earlier, with asthenon), so the omission cannot account for the ASV's phrase.
